# The post-mortem of 28 October: final report

## How to read this

- Times are UTC; yours is UTC+1. A time with seconds, such as 13:00:30, is a message in the session transcript. `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py` prints any message of yours by its time.
- "The account" is `account.md` beside this report, the analysis of 28 October. Evidence files are in `evidence/` beside it, named by file name. Other paths start at `explorations/`.
- POSITIONS holds your decisions, one entry each, such as P-37. FACTS holds what is established about the tree, such as F-293. Each has a history file that keeps every earlier text of an entry and why it changed.
- "The coordinator" is the coordinating session. A worker is an agent that it launches. Sonnet, Opus and Fable are model tiers. A compaction replaces the session's context with a summary; a boot is the session's start-up reading after one. A page is a web page that the coordinator publishes for you to read and comment on.
- A sentence that starts "My reading:" is my own judgement. Every other sentence states what a cited source says.

## In short

- **What failed.** On 26 October a run of the clarity workflow rewrote 13 POSITIONS entries, and you rejected every text. The clarity workflow is the tool that rewrites record entries so that each reads on its own and keeps its meaning.
- **Why.** The steps up to the run were right. The brief that the coordinator wrote for the run made a worker's list binding over the tool's own rules. The deeper cause, found on 29 October: a worker's report was taken as the plan, with no judgement between report and action.
- **What was done.** The tool was restored and given a findings input at your yes. The corrections ran as a pilot of four entries and two chunks (groups of entries) of seven. Your reading found the next fault: every finding had gone into the entry's text. The findings were sorted by home and by weight, one Opus writer wrote the changes from your comments, and they landed at 13:02 on 29 October.
- **What it taught.** A small pilot that you read was the only check of form that worked. Each finding has a home, and the entry's text is only one. A review that reports every fault needs a sort by significance before anything is written.
- **What is open.** Part 2 of the salvage, three answers of the evening not yet in the record, the skill changes on their branch, and some upkeep (section 7).

## 1. What happened on 26 and 27 October

- The phase 3 exit review is the review that you ordered on 24 October, before the switch-over (the step at which the compiled path starts to use the interpreter's library). On 26 October its foundations round checked the nine tenets, the project's base decisions, against the team's sources (`evidence/exit-review-records.md`).

Fortress revival · timeline · 3 November 2026

The record and the skills, 17 October to 3 November

You asked for this on 3 November at 18:20 UTC, 19:20 your time, because the closing docket still lists eight open points about how you and the coordinator work. The coordinator is the Claude session that you talk to. The closing docket is the list of open items that a worker wrote on 3 November.

Six sections

  1. The two post-mortems
  2. The corrections page
  3. The skill drafts page
  4. What stayed open, and why
  5. The revival page
  6. The cleaner pass

1 of 6The two post-mortems

A post-mortem is a review of what went wrong. There were two in these weeks.

The Haiku post-mortem, 19 October

Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable are model tiers, and Haiku is the smallest. On 16 October at 20:09 (22:09 yours), your phone app sent a switch to Haiku with one of your messages. The coordinator then ran on Haiku for three days, for 683 replies. You saw it on 19 October at 21:04 (23:04 yours), and at 21:15 you wrote: “This is a disaster. I never intentionally switched to Haiku and I have noticed only now.” You asked for “thorough Opus reviewers, then one Fable pass.”

What it ruled: the Fable pass kept the code of climb batches 17 and 18, so no rung was redone. It faulted the words: asks for a go that a standing go already covered, a wrong ask on the integer power, and reports that changed the workers' texts. Four lessons landed in the skills that night. To land is to commit to the main branch. The lessons are the model check, the switch that silences the git-check reminders, quiet times, and the rule that a line on the held list is never your yes. The held list is the list of points that you raise while you read. You said “Yes to both rules.” at 23:32 (01:32 yours), after they had landed.

An ask is a message that puts one decision to you. This post-mortem had ten asks.

  • You answered asks 1 to 5 on 19 and 20 October: the relaunch of two workers, the integer power, the array sites, list order, and symbolic operators. The last four became the entries P-153, P-40, P-154 and P-155 of POSITIONS, the file of your decisions.
  • You didn't answer asks 6 to 10. Ask 6 is who decides changes to the coordinator skill. Ask 7 is the AnyList of P-151, and ask 8 is an object's value parameters under a conditional extension. Both wait in the review queue at their defaults. A default is the option that stands until you choose. Ask 9 is a page for each landing, and ask 10 is a push notification that names its batch.
  • On 20 October at 12:07 (14:07 yours) you wrote: “Some of these don't ring a bell, so will you bring them up one by one”. The coordinator had written at 06:23 that asks 6, 9 and 10 stay open, as questions about how you work.

The post-mortem of 28 October

On 26 October the clarity workflow rewrote 13 entries of POSITIONS. The clarity workflow is the tool that rewrites record entries so that each reads on its own. You rejected every text at 19:08 (21:08 yours): “It is in the Claude speak. It is not in the ASD-STE100 register.” On 28 October at 07:42 (08:42 yours) you asked: “This last one was an utter failure. What went wrong?”

What it ruled: the coordinator's brief for the run had overridden the tool's own instructions. The deeper cause was that a worker's report was taken as the plan, with no judgement between the report and the action.

It had five asks.

  • The tool: at 20:42 you chose the clarity workflow with three additions.
  • The pilot, a first small run that you read before the rest: at 21:12 you said “a pilot should be 3-4 entries, not 9”. At 23:09 you left the rest to the coordinator's judgement.
  • The findings that touch your decisions became questions. You answered most of them on 29 October, and P-146 still waits.
  • The quiz, a test with made-up cases: “Yes to the five, go”, at 21:40.
  • Three proposals for the skills: not answered. At 22:02 you asked whether a shortened procedure was meant, and your reply at 23:07 didn't choose. The proposals sit on a side branch that was never merged, and five lessons of this post-mortem are in no skill.
References
  1. The Haiku post-mortem: its report, sections 1 to 5; fable-judgement.md lines 157 to 171. Transcript: 19 October 21:04:25, 21:15:29, 21:40:04, 23:32:52; 20 October 06:23:52, 12:07:28. Asks 7 and 8: review-queue items 188 and 177.
  2. The post-mortem of 28 October: its report, lines 28 and 96 to 102; account.md lines 210 to 227. Transcript: 26 October 19:08:27; 28 October 20:42:16, 21:12:23, 21:40:25, 22:02:55, 23:07:04, 23:09:32. The branch skill/consolidation-tools; the docket, section 2, item 1.

2 of 6The foundations review and the corrections page

On 26 October the foundations review checked the project's nine base decisions against the team's sources. Its page, Foundations Corrections Baseline, went through 16 versions. A page is a web page that the coordinator publishes for you to read and comment on.

  • 26 October, versions 1 to 3: the 13 rewritten entries that you rejected.
  • 28 and 29 October, versions 4 to 10: a pilot of four entries, then 16 entries, each shown as a change to its current text. On 29 October at 05:49 (06:49 yours) you wrote that the corrections went into the “wrong part of the record. Some of them belong to history, some to FACTS.” At 13:00 you wrote: “The text of positions after rewrite seems good to me”. At 13:02 the 16 entries landed: P-7, P-9, P-12, P-25, P-27, P-33, P-37, P-44, P-48, P-58, P-59, P-84, P-152, P-153, P-154 and P-158.
  • 29 October, version 11: three questions for climb batch 22c. Your answers changed P-155, P-33 and P-58. On 30 October your word of 09:27 made P-26 name the POPL 2019 paper.
  • 30 October, version 12: eleven corrections that bring entries in line with the tree. On 31 October at 08:19 (09:19 yours) you said: “you don't need my approval to bring the record in line with reality.” At 08:39 ten entries landed: P-39, P-42, P-45, P-58, P-68, P-79, P-146, P-154, P-156 and P-158. The two questions on P-42 stay yours.
  • 2 November, versions 13 to 16: your choice at 12:37 on the team's later word changed P-7, P-26 and P-37. At 16:42 (17:42 yours) you wrote: “The rewording of P7 and P26 as worded in the latest revision 15 is accepted.” It landed at 16:46. At 18:04 your decision kept the tuple rule of P-156.

3 of 6The skill drafts page

A skill is a file of instructions that Claude loads, and the coordinator skill holds how the coordinator works with you and with the workers. The skill drafts page carried the held rules, the rules that you stated about how you and the coordinator work, as drafts for that skill. It went through eight versions, and five commits landed its rules.

  • 30 October, versions 1 and 2: 20 rules and three proposals of the coordinator's.
  • 31 October, version 3: 22 rules. On 1 November you left 12 comments, and at 23:35 (00:35 yours) you wrote: “Everything that I did not comment on is accepted by default.” Seven minutes later, the ten rules that you hadn't commented on landed, with three proposals of the coordinator's.

  • 2 November, versions 5 and 6: the redrafts and three new drafts, 33 items in all. At 22:03 the rest landed: your LGTMs, the rules reworded for your comments, and the fixes of a cold read, a reading by a worker that sees the text fresh.
  • 2 November at 23:19 and 23:46, versions 7 and 8: what landed, with 13 items as drafted, 15 changed and 4 left out, and the skill writer's three decisions not taken. The skill writer is the worker that drafts skill text.
  • 3 November at 06:29: after your answer of 06:10, the held-list rule landed.
